choices.text: count(1) is quicker, as there is no column for it to inspect

choices.text: An aggregate function is what a GROUP BY admits beside itself

choices.text: The comparison would require the whole table to be held in memory

choices.text: It does work a WHERE would have skipped

prompt: Adding ORDER BY inside OVER changes the number the function returns. Why?

choices.why: That is what RANGE does with peers, and it is not what the ORDER BY does.

choices.why: With an ORDER BY the frame ends at the current row, so the total accumulates.

choices.text: It sorts the rows, and a sum follows whatever order the rows are in

prompt: Why does lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) beat joining the table to itself on month - 1?
hint: Imagine a month in which nothing was sold.

choices.text: A self-join has to be wrapped in a subquery to be written
choices.why: It can, and people do; the trouble is what it does with a gap.

choices.text: It avoids reading the table, which the self-join has to do twice
choices.why: It reads the table once, which is a real gain and not the important one.

choices.text: It is the one of the two that can compute a difference
choices.why: A self-join computes differences perfectly well when the rows are all there.

choices.text: It works when a month is missing
choices.why: lag takes the previous row that exists, where the join finds nothing to pair.
